[TUSTARI:2:30#2/r4] TUSTARI, d. 283 · author | holds | Before creation God decreed that a heart settled on anything besides Him would face Satan's whisper through desire, while the person could instead return in refuge; Adam's deed became a lesson in his descendants through the Last Day.
[TUSTARI:2:30#2/r5] TUSTARI, d. 283 · author | holds | Eating was not the real point: God meant that Adam should not let his aspiration settle on anything other than Him.
[TUSTARI:2:30#2/r6] TUSTARI, d. 283 · author | holds | Anyone who claims what is not theirs and settles inwardly on its desire risks divine abandonment, unless God mercies them by protecting them from self-management and aiding them against Satan and the ego.
[TUSTARI:2:30#2/r7] TUSTARI, d. 283 · author | holds | Paradise's people are protected from the self-management of worldly life; Adam was not protected from planning for permanence, so appetite and desire overpowered knowledge, reason, clarity, and the heart's light by prior decree.
[TUSTARI:2:30#2/r8] TUSTARI, d. 283 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet is quoted as saying that desire and appetite overcome knowledge and reason, explaining Adam's susceptibility to temptation.
[TUSTARI:2:30#3/r1] TUSTARI, d. 283 · author | holds | The angels mean that they purify themselves by uttering what God graciously inspired them to say.
[TUSTARI:2:30/r1] TUSTARI, d. 283 · author | holds | Before Adam's creation, God announced to the angels that He would install him as a vicegerent on earth.
[TUSTARI:2:30/r2] TUSTARI, d. 283 · author | holds | Adam was made from clay of divine might and from the light of Muhammad.

[TAB-FULL:v1p466/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · بعض المنسوبين إلى العلم بلغات العرب من أهل البصرة | reports | A Basran language scholar says the opening means And your Lord said, treating idh as an extra particle with no meaning; he adduces poems by al-Aswad b. Yaʿfur and ʿAbd Manāf al-Hudhalī.
[TAB-FULL:v1p466/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | rejects | Tabari rejects deleting idh: it can function conditionally and indicate an unspecified time, so a particle that gives the sentence meaning cannot be declared superfluous.
[TAB-FULL:v1p466/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | rejects | In al-Aswad b. Yaʿfur's line, fa-idhā points to the present situation and the preceding life; removing idh would destroy the poem's sense.
[TAB-FULL:v1p466/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | rejects | In ʿAbd Manāf b. Rabīʿ's line, idhā introduces a condition whose consequence is omitted but understood; removing it would break the meaning.
[TAB-FULL:v1p466/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Arabic also omits recoverable words after expressions such as wherever, before and after, and if a brother honors you; the surviving wording still signals what is omitted.
[TAB-FULL:v1p469/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | A further poem beginning fa-idhā wa-dhālika provides another parallel for the meaningful use of idhā in al-Aswad b. Yaʿfur's line.
[TAB-FULL:v1p469/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Tabari links this clause to the preceding rebuke: the audience is implicitly told to remember God's favors in creating them and the earth, and to remember His act toward their father Adam. | mentions 2:28, 2:29
[TAB-FULL:v1p471/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | In the cited poem, wa-lā mutadārik has no preceding overt verb to coordinate with; it is governed by the implied sense of the earlier negated phrase.
[TAB-FULL:v1p471/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The poem means I am not seeing; mutadārik is coordinated with the syntactic position of tarā as if the omitted laisa and bi- were expressed.
[TAB-FULL:v1p471/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Likewise, idh in this verse attaches to the implied command to remember in the preceding clause, coordinating by its meaning rather than an overt matching form. | mentions 2:28

[TAB-FULL:v1p472/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Arabic often alternates between a hamzated root form and an unhamzated derived form, as in raʾaytu beside narā, tarā, and yarā.
[TAB-FULL:v1p472/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Malak may also be pronounced maʾlak by metathesis, like the paired forms jabadh/jadhab and shaʾmal/shamʾal.

[TAB-FULL:v1p472/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The root meaning of malāʾak is a message or dispatch; ʿAdī b. Zayd uses it for a message sent to al-Nuʿmān.

[TAB-FULL:v1p475#2/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A report attributed to the Prophet says the earth was spread from Mecca, angels first circumambulated the House, and it was the earth meant here; surviving prophets and their followers later worshipped there, with several prophets’ graves between Zamzam and the Black Stone and Station.

[TAB-FULL:v1p477/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · الربيع بن أنس | reports | Al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas says angels were created Wednesday, jinn Thursday, and Adam Friday; when some jinn disbelieved, angels fought them, producing bloodshed and corruption on earth.

[TAB-FULL:v1p500/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | If God had disclosed the future corruption, Al-Tabari says the angels could be asking whether it would in fact occur and asking God to make them earth’s deputies so that no one would disobey.
[TAB-FULL:v1p500/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · الضحاك عن ابن عباس والربيع بن أنس | reports | Al-Dahhak, from Ibn Abbas and also followed by al-Rabi b. [TAB-FULL:v1p500/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | rejects | Al-Tabari does not call the prior-jinn account or Ibn Zayd’s astonishment account impossible, but sets both aside because no sufficiently authoritative report establishes them.
[TAB-FULL:v1p500/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن زيد | reports | Ibn Zayd interprets the angels’ question as amazement that God would create beings who disobey their creator, rather than as knowledge that this would certainly occur.
[TAB-FULL:v1p500/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Tabari says knowledge of past events is reliable only through transmission that rules out collusion, lying, error and forgetfulness; the cited reports do not meet that standard, so the text-supported interpretation is preferable.

[ZAJJAJ:v1p108/r4] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · قيل | reports | A people called jinn lived on earth, corrupted it and shed blood; God sent angels to drive them away, and the angels then inhabited earth.

[ZAJJAJ:v1p109/r3] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Safaka means to pour or spill something.

[ZAJJAJ:v1p109/r5] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Any act intended for God may be called tasbīḥ; completing prayer is one Arabic use of tasbīḥ.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p109/r6] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · سيبويه وغيره من النحويين | reports | Sībawayh and other grammarians gloss subḥān Allāh as declaring God free of evil and exalting Him above it.

[NAHHAS:v1p206/r10] NAHHAS, d. 338 · أبو إسحاق | reports | Abū Isḥāq connects the mention of human and other creation to an implied beginning: their creation began when the Lord spoke to the angels.
[NAHHAS:v1p206/r11] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | «الملائكة» is genitive after the lām; the group is grammatically feminine.
[NAHHAS:v1p206/r12] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | The yāʾ in «إني» is accusative and «جاعل» is the predicate of «إن»; the original «إنني» loses a nūn where two meet.
[NAHHAS:v1p206/r13] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | «الأرض» is genitive after «في», while «خليفة» is accusative after «جاعل».
[NAHHAS:v1p206/r14] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | «خليفة» is the object of «جاعل»; its tanwīn cannot be omitted with the intervening phrase, though it could if the object immediately followed.
[NAHHAS:v1p206/r15] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | reports | «خليفة» may be active: one who succeeds the angels or other predecessors in the earth, as also related.
[NAHHAS:v1p206/r16] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | reports | Alternatively «خليفة» may be passive, one who is succeeded.
[NAHHAS:v1p206/r17] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | «أتجعل» is a future verb.
[NAHHAS:v1p206/r18] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | «من يفسد» is accusative as the first object of «تجعل»; «فيها» supplies the second object's position on the singular wording.
[NAHHAS:v1p206/r19] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | reports | Outside the Qurʾānic wording, the plural «يفسدون» is possible by sense.
[NAHHAS:v1p206/r20] NAHHAS, d. 338 · الأعرج | reports | Al-Aʿraj is reported to read «ويسفك الدماء» with «الدماء» in the accusative as the answer to the question introduced by wāw.
[NAHHAS:v1p206/r21] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | The singular of «الدماء» is «دم»; no noun has only two letters without an omitted letter, here a yāʾ retained in poetic usage.
[NAHHAS:v1p206/r22] NAHHAS, d. 338 · الشاعر | reports | An unnamed poet's «الدميان» shows the original yāʾ in the dual form of «دم».
[NAHHAS:v1p206/r23] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | The nūn cannot be assimilated into the following nūn because the result would put two quiescent consonants together.
[NAHHAS:v1p206/r24] NAHHAS, d. 338 · من حرك الياء | reports | Those who vocalize the yāʾ in «إني» avoid leaving a one-letter noun without a vowel.
[NAHHAS:v1p206/r25] NAHHAS, d. 338 · من أسكنها | reports | Those who leave the yāʾ quiescent say it has joined to what precedes it.
[NAHHAS:v1p206/r26] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | reports | «أعلم» can be a present verb or a participle meaning “knowing,” as «الله أكبر» can mean “God is great.”
[NAHHAS:v1p206/r9] NAHHAS, d. 338 · أبو عبيدة | reports | Abū ʿUbayda says «إذ» is a temporal adverb and is not an extra word.
[NAHHAS:v1p208/r1] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | An unattributed poetic line occurs in the preceding discussion of ما; the excerpt gives no poet or explicit gloss for the line.
[NAHHAS:v1p208/r2] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | Mīm may assimilate into mīm. ما is accusative with أعلم if verbal; if nominal, it may be genitive by annexation or accusative, with tanwīn dropped because the form is diptote.
[IBNHIBBAN:6186/r1] IBNHIBBAN, d. 354 · ابن عمر | reports | Ibn ʿUmar reports that after Adam descended, angels questioned humanity’s corruption; God tested Hārūt and Mārūt on earth, where a woman’s demands led them to shirk, drunkenness, sex, and murder before they chose worldly punishment.
[IBNHIBBAN:6186/r2] IBNHIBBAN, d. 354 · أبو حاتم | holds | Abū Ḥātim clarifies that the woman called al-Zuhara was a human woman of that time, not the celestial planet Venus.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p74/r1] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · author | holds | Opening the possessive yāʾ treats it as a built pronoun like hāʾ or kāf; the vowel is fitting after the preceding kasra.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p74/r2] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · author | holds | Sukūn avoids the heaviness of a vowel on yāʾ and restores the pronoun's underlying built form.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p74/r3] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · القراء | reports | One group opens yāʾ before a hamza with fatḥa but uses sukūn before ḍamma or kasra, avoiding those heavier vowel combinations.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p74/r4] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · القراء | reports | Another group uses sukūn before ḍamma, the heaviest vowel, but opens yāʾ before the other hamzas.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p74/r5] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · القراء | reports | A third group deletes the possessive yāʾ entirely and relies on the remaining vowel.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p74/r6] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · author | holds | When attached to a one-letter word, opening yāʾ is preferable so elision at two adjacent sukūns does not leave a one-letter word; sukūn remains permissible.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p74/r7] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · author | holds | Arabic permits four possessive-yāʾ forms: opening, sukūn, adding an alif to soften the vowel, or deleting the yāʾ for brevity.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p411#2/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو عمرو | reports | Abū ʿAmr opens the attached yāʾ after a kasra before an open or kasra hamza; this rule includes إني أعلم.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p411#2/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو عمرو | reports | He does not open the yāʾ before a hamza with ḍamma, as in the cited examples; his opening rule is restricted to the open and kasra hamza.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p411#2/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · ابن كثير | reports | Ibn Kathīr does not follow one consistent rule for these attached yāʾ vowels; his individual cases are listed separately by sūra.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p413/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | The case for opening the attached yāʾ is that its original vowel is fatḥa, parallel to the addressee kāf, which is also opened.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p413/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Although vowels on weak letters are often avoided, fatḥa is acceptable: yāʾ in al-qāḍī is inflected with fatḥa, and accusative غَوَاشٍ retains its yāʾ.

item.text: The early sources cluster around the meaning of “successor,” how the angels knew about corruption, whether their question was an inquiry, and what God’s answer reveals. I’m keeping the grammatical, reading, report, and inward interpretations alongside those themes.

[TABRISI:2:30/r11] TABRISI, d. 548 · ابن كيسان | reports | Ibn Kaysan derives it from الملك: ملأك is فعال like شمأل, ملائكة is فعائلة, the mīm is original, and hamza added.
[TABRISI:2:30/r12] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Though “angel” originally meant messenger, it became the established label for God's nonhuman messengers, as “heaven” came to name the familiar skies.
[TABRISI:2:30/r13] TABRISI, d. 548 · أصحابنا | reports | The author's companions say not all angels are messengers, citing 22:75; if all were messengers all would be selected, so ملك is generic rather than derived from message. | mentions 22:75
[TABRISI:2:30/r14] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | جعل, خلق, فعل, and إحداث are related, but جعل can assign a state without creating; فعل and إحداث mean bringing into existence.
[TABRISI:2:30/r15] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | خليفة and إمام overlap in use but differ: a khalifa succeeds a predecessor, while an imam leads and is to be followed and obeyed.
[TABRISI:2:30/r16] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | سفك means pouring out blood; grammarians disagree whether دم follows فعل or فعِل.
[TABRISI:2:30/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | رب is traced to ربيته, managing someone's affairs; a rabbani scholar manages the community's affairs.
[TABRISI:2:30/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · أكثر العلماء والخليل | reports | Most scholars derive angels from الألوكة, “message”; al-Khalil defines ألوك as message and gives the related form مألكة.
[TABRISI:2:30/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · غيره | reports | Another etymology says a message is called ألوكة because it is chewed in the mouth, like a horse chewing its bridle.
[TABRISI:2:30/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · عدي بن زيد | reports | Adi ibn Zayd's مألكا in his poem witnesses the message derivation.
[TABRISI:2:30/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · لبيد | reports | Labid's ألوك in his poem witnesses the message derivation.
[TABRISI:2:30/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · الهذلي | reports | The Hudhali poet's ألكني in his verse is another witness to the message derivation.
[TABRISI:2:30/r8] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | On the message derivation, ملائكة is a reversed plural of ملأك meaning messenger; a poem attests the hamzated form.
[TABRISI:2:30/r9] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Some Arabs keep the hamza, but most shift its vowel to the lām and drop it, saying ملك.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p58#2/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · أبو عبيدة وابن قتيبة | reports | Abū ʿUbayda, followed by Ibn Qutayba, treats idh as redundant, yielding ‘and your Lord said.’
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p58#2/r10] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الحسن | reports | Al-Hasan says God announced Adam’s creation to test the angels’ obedience.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p58#2/r11] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن زيد | reports | Ibn Zayd says the angels feared after God created fire and told them it was for those who disobeyed; they feared they might disobey, so God announced the earthly khalīfa.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p58#2/r12] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | reports | God informed the angels to show that their knowledge could not encompass His wisdom, which they acknowledged in their question.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p58#2/r13] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | reports | God mentioned Adam’s future vicegerency before his creation to honor him and ensure the angels would revere him if He brought him into being.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p58#2/r14] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | reports | God meant to tell the angels that Adam would inhabit earth, even though his initial creation took place in heaven.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p58#2/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الزجاج وابن القاسم | rejects | Al-Zajjāj and Ibn al-Qāsim reject the claim that idh is redundant; al-Zajjāj takes it to mean ‘at the time’ of the beginning of creation.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p58#2/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Malāʾika derives from al-ūlūk, meaning a message; Labīd’s line about a mother sending a message is evidence.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p58#2/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The singular of malāʾika is malak, originally malʾak, as Sibawayh’s verse demonstrates.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p58#2/r5] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · أبو إسحاق | reports | Abū Isḥāq glosses malʾak as ‘bearer of a message’; related forms include maʾlaka and malʾaka, with maʾālik as a plural, illustrated by a poem to al-Nuʿmān.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p58#2/r6] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · السدي عن أشياخه | reports | One view takes the angels addressed as all the angels.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p58#2/r7] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن عباس | reports | The other view identifies them as the angels with Iblīs when he was sent down to earth; Abū Ṣāliḥ transmits this from Ibn ʿAbbās.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p58#2/r8] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | reports | It is related that creatures lived on earth before Adam, caused corruption, and were destroyed by Iblīs and a company of angels sent by God.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p58#2/r9] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن عباس والسدي عن أشياخه | reports | God knew Iblīs harbored pride and disobedience and wished to reveal it to the angels; this is related from Ibn ʿAbbās and by al-Suddī from his elders.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p60/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن الأنباري | reports | Khalīfa means one who succeeds another; Ibn al-Anbārī says its original form was khalīf, with the feminine ending added to intensify praise, like ʿallāma and nasāba.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p60/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن مسعود ومجاهد | reports | One view says Adam is God’s deputy for establishing His law, signs of His oneness, and judgment among His creation.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p60/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن عباس والحسن | reports | The other view says Adam succeeded earlier inhabitants of the earth.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p60/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | reports | One analysis takes the interrogative alif as emphatic confirmation, not a genuine question; Jarīr’s line uses a question to assert that the addressees are best.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p60/r5] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjāj says the angels asked to learn the wisdom behind the decision, not as an objection.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p60/r6] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | reports | A third reading makes the angels ask about their own standing: will God place a corrupting creature there while they glorify Him, or not?
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p60/r7] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن مسعود وابن عباس والحسن ومجاهد وقتادة وابن زيد وابن قتيبة | reports | These authorities hold that God had informed the angels the khalīfa’s descendants would corrupt; al-Suddī reports they were told the descendants would envy and kill one another.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p60/r8] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن عباس وأبي العالية ومقاتل | reports | The alternative view is that the angels inferred the corruption from the condition of those who had lived before Adam.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p61#2/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن عباس ومجاهد والسدي عن أشياخه | reports | One interpretation is that God knows the pride and disobedience within Iblīs; this is attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and al-Suddī from his elders.

[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p61#2/r8] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says the breath entered Adam through his head, and each part it reached became flesh and blood.

[RAZI-FULL:v1p88/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · آخرون | reports | Others hold that the partitive use is primary and that min's other uses derive from it.

[RAZI-FULL:v2p146#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · بعض الناس | reports | One view treats إذ as an extra particle customary in Arabic; Razi rejects it because the Qur'an contains nothing without meaning.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p146#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | prefers | Razi's preferred analysis makes إذ accusative through an implied اذكر: remember that your Lord said this to the angels; the omission is clear from context.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p146#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Other passages state اذكر explicitly, and the Qur'an functions as one discourse, so their explicit wording can suffice here; they may have preceded this sura. | mentions 46:21, 38:17, 36:13, 36:14

[RAZI-FULL:v2p146#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The word ملك derives from a root meaning message: ألكني إليه means send me to him, and المألكة or الألوكة means a message.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p146#2/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The original form ملأكة lost its hamza, whose vowel shifted to the preceding letter for ease because the word was frequent.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p146#2/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · صاحب الكشاف | reports | Al-Kashshaf derives الملائك as the plural of the original ملأك, like شمائل from شمأل, with feminine plural تاء.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p147/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · بعض الناس | reports | Those who put angels before prophets cite 2:285's order of belief and the Prophet's instruction to begin with what God began with. | mentions 2:285
[RAZI-FULL:v2p147/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · بعض الناس | reports | They also argue angels precede prophets because angels mediate revelation and the law to the messengers.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p147/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · بعض الناس | reports | Others put prophethood first because reason alone cannot establish angels; revelation, grounded in knowledge of prophethood, is the route to affirming them.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p147/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | prefers | Razi reconciles the sequence: angels precede prophets in rank and nobility, but follow them in our reasoning because we establish angels through inquiry.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p147/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Rationalists agree that angels ennoble the upper world, just as humans ennoble the lower world.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p147/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أكثر المسلمين | reports | Most Muslims hold that angels are subtle airy bodies, able to take different forms, and dwelling in the heavens.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p147/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · طوائف من عبدة الأوثان | reports | Some idol worshippers identify angels with the actual planetary natures they deem auspicious or inauspicious: auspicious planets are mercy angels and inauspicious ones punishment angels.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p147/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · معظم المجوس والثنوية | reports | Most Magians and dualists posit two eternal, transparent, choosing substances, Light and Darkness, opposite in nature and action; Light is good and beneficial, Darkness its contrary.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p147/r9] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · معظم المجوس والثنوية | reports | In their account, Light continually generates angels as friends without sexual reproduction, like wisdom from a wise person; Darkness similarly generates devils as enemies.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p148#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · عليه الصلاة والسلام | reports | A Prophetic report says the heavens groan, rightly so, for every space the size of a foot contains an angel prostrating or bowing; Razi gives no grading.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p148#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | A report gives successive tenfold ratios from humans and jinn through land, bird, and sea animals to earthly angels and the angels of each heaven, up to the angels of the Throne's pavilion; even all those angels are a drop beside those circling the Throne.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p148#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | The report describes 600,000 Throne pavilions, angels in every footspace worshipping, and numberless ranks whose species, lifespans, and worship only God knows.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p148#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | In a report Razi saw in an admonition book, the Prophet at the Ascension met angels moving like a marketplace; Gabriel did not know their destinations and had never seen the same angel twice.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p148#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · ملك | reports | In that report, an angel could not say how long he had existed, only that God had created a star every 400,000 years and that many such stars had appeared since his creation.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p148/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · طوائف من النصارى | reports | Some Christians identify angels with disembodied rational souls: purified, good souls are angels, while evil, clouded souls are devils.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p148/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الفلاسفة | reports | Philosophers describe angels as self-subsisting, nonspatial substances distinct from human souls and greater in power and knowledge, as the Sun is to its light.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p148/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الفلاسفة | reports | They divide angels into celestial governors, related to spheres as human souls to bodies, and proximate angels absorbed in knowing, loving, and obeying God; some add good or evil angels governing the lower world.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p148/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الفلاسفة | reports | Philosophers agree on celestial governors and angels devoted to God, while some also posit terrestrial angels governing the lower world, good as angels and evil as devils.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p148/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الفلاسفة | reports | Philosophers affirm rational proofs of angels' existence; Razi says he has deep, subtle discussions of their arguments, while other people offer merely persuasive proofs.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p148/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · بعض الناس | reports | One proof divides living beings into mortal rational humans, mortal nonrational beasts, and rational immortal angels; if wisdom creates the lower and middle ranks, it should create the highest too.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p148/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · بعض الناس | reports | Another proof says the celestial world is nobler and life, intellect, and speech nobler than their opposites, so it is implausible that these exist only in the dark lower world.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p148/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أصحاب المجاهدات وأصحاب الحاجات والضرورات | reports | A third proof invokes mystics' witnessing and unveiling, remarkable guidance for rare treatments and antidotes, and true dreams; it persuades hearers and is certain to those who experience it.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p148/r9] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الأنبياء عليهم السلام | holds | Razi says all prophets agree on the existence of angels, a matter of consensus among them, established by transmitted reports.

[QASHANI:2:30#2/r3] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Each angelic rank knows what is below and within itself but not above; they see the soul as evil-bearing intermediary between luminous spirit and dark body.
[QASHANI:2:30#2/r4] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | The angels do not know that human comprehensiveness attracts divine light, the secret of God's statement that He knows what they do not.
[QASHANI:2:30#2/r5] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Glorification denies partner, incapacity, and defect; sanctification also denies attachment, passivity, contingency, multiplicity, and potentiality, so every sanctified being glorifies but not vice versa.
[QASHANI:2:30#2/r6] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | The nearest angels, pure spirits, are sanctifiers because they are un-veiled, overcome lower realms with light, act on others, and possess all perfections actually; other angels glorify.
[QASHANI:2:30/r1] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | The time reference points to eternity; God's saying casts His will to create Adam into sacred angelic and spiritual beings.
[QASHANI:2:30/r2] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Every created event first has a form in the spirit world of prior decree, then the heart-world of the Preserved Tablet, then the soul-world, Tablet of Effacement and Affirmation or lowest heaven. | mentions 15:21
[QASHANI:2:30/r3] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Human speech and action similarly exist first in spirit and deeper unseen levels, then the self's lower unseen level, before appearing on the limbs.
[QASHANI:2:30/r4] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Making is broader than origination or formation, so God says 'making' rather than 'creating'; the human combines the two worlds.
[QASHANI:2:30/r5] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | The human vicegerent takes on God's traits, executes His command, governs creation, orders its affairs, and calls people to obedience.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p221#2/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Idh is a built temporal noun for past time, built because it resembles a particle in form or need.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p221#2/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Another derivation makes the first radical hamza and the second lām from al-ʾalūka, message; māʾlak was inverted into malʾak.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p221#2/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | A third derivation links malak to lāka, to roll something in the mouth; the messenger carries a message in the mouth, with the middle radical deleted for ease.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p221#2/r12] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | On the third derivation, malāʾika is mufāʿala and its hamza replaces wāw, as in maṣāʾib.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p221#2/r13] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · النضر بن شميل | reports | Al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl says Arabs neither derive nor inflect malak, whose etymology has escaped knowledge.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p221#2/r14] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | The tāʾ in malāʾika marks a feminine plural, or, according to another view, intensification; poetry uses the form without tāʾ.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p221#2/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | After idh comes a nominal or verbal clause; with a verbal clause, fronting its subject and annexing idh to a present-initial clause are poor usage.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p221#2/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | A present verb governed by idh is made past in meaning; idh remains adverbial unless another time noun is annexed to it.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p221#2/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | Idh cannot be an object, causal or sudden particle, locative adverb, or redundant word, contrary to claims that it has those uses.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p221#2/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو عبيدة | reports | Abu Ubayda treats the mīm in malak as original, derives it from strength, and calls its plural malāʾika on faʿāʾila anomalous.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p221#2/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | A competing account supposes malak came from malāk on faʿʿāl, although masculine and feminine faʿʿāl plurals on faʿāʾil are uncommon.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p221#2/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | One analysis reconstructs the original form as faʿʾal like shamʾal, then transfers the vowel and deletes letters; malʾak is also attested.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p221#2/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | One derivation connects malak to lāka, to send: the original was malʾak, reduced by moving the vowel and deleting, with malāʾika on mufāʿala.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p221#2/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو عبيدة | reports | Abu Ubayda gives the malʾak derivation, which Abū al-Fatḥ also selects; on this account malāʾika is mufāʿala.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p222/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | An unnamed poet uses malāʾik without the tāʾ found in the ordinary plural malāʾika.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p222/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Khalīfa is on faʿīla, which can be an intensive active form like al-ʿalīm or a passive form like al-naṭīḥa; its tāʾ can intensify.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p222/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Safk means pouring or spilling and is used only of blood; safaka, safika, and asfaka share the same meaning, with two present-tense patterns.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p222/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Damāʾ is the plural of dam; its omitted final weak radical may be yāʾ or wāw, as shown by damiyān and damwān.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p222/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | The language also attests shortening and consonant doubling for dam, while grammarians differ over the deleted radical's original vowel pattern.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p222/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Tasbīḥ means declaring God free of evil, is used only for God, and derives from sabḥ, running; the one who glorifies runs in that declaration.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p223/r15] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو عبيدة | reports | Abū ʿUbayda and Ibn Qutayba take idh as redundant; Abū Ḥayyān rejects this and criticizes their grammatical competence.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p223/r16] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | An alternative reads idh as qad, yielding wa-qad qāla rabbuka, but Abū Ḥayyān rejects it.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p223/r17] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | Some parse idh as an object of an unspoken udhkur, but this wrongly removes it from its temporal-adverbial function.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p224/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, and others permit construing idh as an object of udhkur, though Abū Ḥayyān rejects that analysis.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p224/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The shift from general address to the Prophet's particular address hints that he receives the greatest share of what follows; Abū Ḥayyān recalls his universal mission and precedence among prophets.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p224/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The lām in lil-malāʾika marks conveying speech, one of the lām's functions.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p224/r12] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | The apparent reading makes the angels general; another group takes them specifically as earthly angels after the jinn or as those who fought with Iblis.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p224/r13] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The predicate after qāla is introduced by anna to stress that the reported statement is certain to occur.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p224/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Some make idh nominative as the beginning of creation; others make it accusative as the beginning of creation occurred when God spoke.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p224/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | Abū Ḥayyān rejects both parses because human creation did not begin when God spoke to the angels, while a temporal predicate must occur within its time adverb.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p224/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | Idh cannot be governed by the following qāla because idh is annexed to that clause, and an annexed complement cannot govern its annexer.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p224/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | Parsing idh under aḥyākum requires unsupported deletion; revival did not occur at that time, and it deletes a relative clause while retaining its complement.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p224/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | Making idh depend on khalaqakum from the earlier command requires a redundant wāw and separates the governor from it with long, syntactically independent verses. | mentions 2:21
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p224/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | Abū Ḥayyān counts

 eight such analyses and says the Qurʾān should be kept clear of them.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p224/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | prefers | He prefers governing idh with qālū: when God says He will place a khalifa, the angels respond, Would You place one there who corrupts? This is clear temporal usage.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p224/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Attributing the speech to the Lord fits the prior mention of provision on earth and honors the Messenger through a special address that introduces humanity's origin and destiny.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p226/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Most Arabs open the hamza in anna after qāla only under stated conditions, while Banū Sulaym do so without conditions; an unnamed poet illustrates their usage.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p226/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الجمهور | reports | The apparent sense of fī al-arḍ is the whole earth, as the majority hold; another view identifies the land as Mecca.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p226/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن سابط | reports | Ibn Sābiṭ transmits the Mecca interpretation as a report traced to the Prophet; Abū Ḥayyān says it should be followed if authentic.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p226/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Jāʿil is an active participle with future force; if it governs its object, that is better than annexation for Sibawayh, while al-Kisāʾī considers both equal and Abū Ḥayyān prefers annexation.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p226/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · سيبويه | reports | Sībawayh says that when the active participle operates, using it as an operative form is better than annexing it to its object.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p226/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الكسائي | reports | Al-Kisāʾī regards the operative and annexed constructions as equal; Abū Ḥayyān chooses annexation as better.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p226/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو روق | reports | One view makes jaʿala mean create, taking one object; Abū Rawq holds this, close to reports from al-Ḥasan and Qatāda.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p226/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الفراء | reports | A second view, held by al-Farrāʾ, makes jaʿala mean turn into, taking two objects, with fī al-arḍ supplying the second; al-Zamakhsharī gives only this view.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p226/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | prefers | Both meanings are possible, but creation is stronger: if the first jaʿala meant appointment, the angels' reply would have explicitly called its object a khalifa.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p226/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | There is no need to supply an omitted khalifa, since wording without ellipsis is better; the active participle conveys a settled state rather than gradual renewal.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p226/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Whether jaʿala means create or appoint, Adam became khalifa only once, so the act was not repeated.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p227#2/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | If the angels addressed are all angels, the statement exposes Iblis's pride and reveals what God already knew; reports are cited from Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Suddī through his teachers.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p227#2/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | He reiterates that the preferred governor of idh is qālū, with the following clause أتجعل as its governed complement.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p227#2/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Because angels neither know the unseen nor speak first, their question must rest on prior information or a premise.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p227#2/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan says the announcement tests the angels' obedience.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p227#2/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Other proposed purposes are to expose angels' inability to encompass God's knowledge and to honor Adam in advance so they welcome him when created.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p227#2/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | The announcement could teach that Adam was created to inhabit earth although his creation began in heaven, and model consulting learned people despite already knowing the answer.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p227#2/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | It could also lead angels to admit and revise assumptions about complete knowledge, show Adam's learning by asking him to name things, or teach obedience without requiring full understanding. | mentions 2:31
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p227#2/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن زيد | reports | Ibn Zayd says the announcement reassured angels who feared the Fire and believed no creatures existed besides themselves; God said it was for those who disobey Him.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p227#2/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أهل الإشارة | reports | Some mystically inclined interpreters see divine care as preceding Adam's sin and surviving it: although disobedience caused expulsion, God did not strip Adam of honor or succession and later accepted him. | mentions 20:122
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p227#2/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | An unnamed poem illustrates how a beloved's many virtues outweigh one fault; another poem likewise says a single lapse should not provoke blame.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p227#2/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Abū Ḥayyān says God singled Adam out by announcing a khalifa, unlike the creation of the heavens, throne, or Paradise, thereby honoring and distinguishing him.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p227/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | An unnamed poem responds to claims that the Hijaz land is recent by saying the speaker seeks nothing beyond the earth.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p227/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عباس | reports | In Ibn ʿAbbās's account, God gave Iblis earthly and lower-heaven sovereignty and Paradise's treasury; pride led him to think he was God's most honored angel, so the announced successor would replace him and his host.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p227/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الجمهور | reports | The majority read khalīfa with fāʾ; it can mean an active successor or one replaced, and in the active sense one entrusted to act in another's place.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p227/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن مسعود وابن عباس | reports | One view identifies the khalifa as Adam, succeeding earthly angels, the jinn, Iblis in earthly rule, or God; Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn ʿAbbās are cited for the last view.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p227/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The prophets are God's successors on earth, and Adam alone is named because he is the forefather of all successors, as tribal names can stand for the whole tribe.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p227/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan says the khalifa is Adam's progeny, each generation replacing another; the singular can represent a collective, as in other Qurʾanic passages. | mentions 6:165, 24:55
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p227/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Another view treats khalifa as the title of anyone entrusted with governing earth's people and overseeing their interests, as Caesar, Kisrā, and Tubbaʿ are royal titles.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p227/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Views differ on Adam's delegated task: judging with truth and justice, or cultivating the earth through farming, construction, and canals.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p227/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · زيد بن علي | reports | Zayd ibn ʿAlī and Abū al-Barahsim ʿImrān read khalīqa with qāf, a variant whose meaning is clear.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p227/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عباس | reports | A report from Ibn ʿAbbās says God first placed angels in heaven and jinn on earth; after the jinn corrupted and fought, Iblis led angels who expelled them and took earthly rule.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p228/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · مكي | reports | The interrogative hamza also conveys astonishment, according to Makkī and others, at God's appointing a successor who would disobey or be disobeyed.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p228/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Another interpretation takes the question as magnifying and honoring the appointment and the resulting disobedience.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p228/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو عبيدة | reports | Abū ʿUbayda reads the question as a request for confirmation, illustrated by an unnamed poet's rhetorical question.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p228/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Under the first three readings, angels' prior knowledge may come from God, the Preserved Tablet, observation of other created beings, analogy with earlier earthly inhabitants, or inference from the word khalifa and its association with injustice.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p228/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أحمد بن يحيى | reports | A fourth view from Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā takes the question plainly: will this successor be like the earlier jinn who inhabited the earth?
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p228/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو الفضل التجلي | reports | Abū al-Faḍl al-Tajallī paraphrases the question as asking whether God will instead appoint one who does not cause corruption.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p228/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Another proposed complement contrasts the question with the angels' state: will You change us, though we glorify You?
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p228/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | For surprise, magnification, or confirmation, the question has no complement; for the plain-question view it is من يفسد, while the other view makes the circumstantial clause its complement.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p228/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الجمهور | reports | The majority read yasfiku with kasra on fāʾ and a nominative kāf; other transmitted readings use ḍamma, the forms from asfaka or doubled safaka, or an accusative kāf from Ibn Hurmuz.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p229/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | The cited poem pairs being bright-eyed with spending a night as if stung, illustrating that the two actions can occur together.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p229/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عطية | reports | Ibn ʿAṭiy

ya calls the accusative a waṣr wāw: the conjunction redirects a verb from its expected mood to accusative, as in other Qurʾanic readings. | mentions 40:56, 3:142
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p229/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | Abū Ḥayyān rejects Ibn ʿAṭiyya's waṣr-wāw analysis because Basran grammarians do not recognize it; they posit an implicit an after wāw, and he criticizes Ibn ʿAṭiyya's preference.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p229/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Because yufsid is affirmative and does not imply every kind of corruption, the angels name bloodshed as the gravest form, which destroys God's created bodies.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p229/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Repeating fīhā after corruption highlights the reversal of a place of worship into one of wrongdoing; the parallel is 2:11, while omission after bloodshed avoids three repetitions. | mentions 2:11
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p229/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The circumstantial clause wa-naḥnu nusabbiḥu has several reported senses: divine transcendence (Qatāda), remembrance aloud (al-Mufaḍḍal), humility (Ibn al-Anbārī), or prayer (Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn ʿAbbās).
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p229/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · مجاهد | reports | Mujāhid interprets tasbīḥ as magnifying God; other views make it a special angelic liturgy or the formula subḥān Allāh wa-bi-ḥamdih.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p230/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · النبي | reports | In a report from ʿUbāda ibn al-Ṣāmit through Abū Dharr, the Prophet says the best words are what God chose for angels or servants: subḥān Allāh wa-bi-ḥamdih.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p230/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Another spiritual interpretation takes taqdīs as cleansing hearts from attention to anything besides God.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p230/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | The lām in laka may be extra, purposive, attached to nuqaddisu or nusabbiḥu, transitive, or explanatory with an omitted taqdīsuna laka; Abū Ḥayyān prefers the transitive function.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p230/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | In bi-ḥamdika, the bāʾ can mark accompaniment: the angels glorify while joined by praise, a circumstantial phrase within another circumstantial phrase.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p230/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Alternatively, bāʾ marks cause: praise arises from enabling and beneficence, so the angels glorify because God grants them good; ḥamd is annexed to its object.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p230/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The Basrans allow omission of the subject in a verbal noun construction; unlike some grammarians, Abū Ḥayyān says this is not forbidden because generic nouns do not take pronouns.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p230/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | There is no need to reorder the phrase as though bi-ḥamdika interrupts wa-nuqaddisu; word order inversion is limited to poetic necessity, and praise naturally accompanies tasbīḥ.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p230/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Wa-nuqaddisu laka reinforces wa-nusabbiḥu because purification and declaring God free of evil are close in meaning.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p230/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الضحاك | reports | Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and others interpret taqdīs as purifying themselves for God from impurities; Abū Muslim instead makes its object their deeds, purified from sins.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p230/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · مجاهد وأبو صالح | reports | Mujāhid and Abū Ṣāliḥ understand taqdīs as magnifying and glorifying God; other reports interpret it as prayer or purification from human deeds.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p230/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عباس | reports | A report attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās says the angels mean that they purify themselves from the deeds of Adam's descendants.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p231/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | He rejects reading the angels’ glorification as a question with an omitted interrogative and an omitted alternative, since the syntax gives no evidence for either deletion.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p231/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Islamic doctrine holds angels immune from sin and objection; this premise led exegetes to interpret their words in a linguistically plausible way, against a minority of Hashwiyya.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p231/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · بعض أهل الإشارات | reports | Some allusive interpreters say the angels thought God had consulted them about keeping the vicegerency with worshippers, so they advised against appointing those who would corrupt and kill; God decides.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p231/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · صفي الدين أبو عبد الله الحسين ابن الوزير أبي الحسن علي بن أبي المنصور الخزرجي | reports | The author of Fakk al-Azrar assigns the apparent objection to Iblis and the glorification and obedience to the angels, who had first spoken in a collective answer.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p231/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | prefers | Abu Hayyan calls that division a good interpretation, analogous to a collective quotation whose different statements belong to different groups. | mentions 2:135
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p231/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قول غير مسمى | reports | One view takes the angels’ self-description as permission to praise one’s qualifications before an appointing authority when seeking office, if one can avoid injustice and sees a benefit.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p232/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The angels’ example permits Joseph to seek office and describe his own qualifications, as he did when asking to oversee Egypt’s storehouses. | mentions 12:55
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p232/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | prefers | He prefers parsing ما after أعلم as a relative pronoun and rejects treating it as an indefinite adjective.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p232/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · مكي بن أبي طالب والمهدوي وغيرهما | reports | Makkī, al-Mahdawī, and others allow أعلم as an active participle; on that parse ما may be genitive by annexation or accusative.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p232/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · بعضهم | reports | Others parse أعلم as a comparative meaning more knowing than you, with ما governed as the object of an implied verb meaning I know.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p233/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | He rejects the proposed comparative parse because it requires omitting both the comparison phrase meaning than you and the verb governing the relative pronoun.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p233/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن زيد | reports | Ibn Zayd says God knew which jinn and humans would fill Hell.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p233/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو عبيدة | reports | Abū ʿUbayda allows أفعل to mean an active participle, but the grammarians reject that analysis; Abu Hayyan sides with the grammarians.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p233/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · النحويون المتقدمون | holds | The earlier grammarians maintain that أفعل always carries a comparative sense, and Abu Hayyan endorses their position.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p233/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · بعض المتأخرين | reports | Some later grammarians allow أفعل to occur without comparison, treating it as an active participle or an adjective of inherent quality.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p233/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو العباس | reports | Abu al-Abbas regards comparative-free use of أفعل as productive, while the cited grammarian says the sounder rule is to limit it to attested usage.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p233/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | Even grammarians who allow comparative-free أفعل do not all let it govern like an active participle; Abu Hayyan rejects inventing such unattested constructions by analogy.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p233/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | He insists that the apparent reading is the present-tense verb أعلم and warns against imposing unattested grammatical patterns on Quranic wording.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p233/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عباس ومجاهد والسدي عن أشياخه | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and al-Suddī from his teachers say God knew what was in Iblis’s mind despite his rebellion and disobedience.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p233/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda says God knew that prophets and righteous people would descend from the vicegerent.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p234/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjāj says God knows outcomes: trials may lead someone thought obedient into sin, or someone thought sinful into obedience.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p234/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قول غير مسمى | reports | Another explanation is God’s complete knowledge of outward and inward matters, subtle and evident, near and distant, good and bad, across changing conditions and times.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p234/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قول غير مسمى | reports | Another explanation contrasts God’s knowledge, gained without acquisition, inquiry, reflection, or thought, with human knowledge.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p234/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قول غير مسمى | reports | One proposed explanation is that God knew Iblis was among the angels addressed.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p234/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قول غير مسمى | reports | One proposed explanation is that God knew the angels were magnifying themselves through their glorification and sanctification.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p234/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The wording leaves unspecified what God knows beyond the angels’ knowledge; that claim requires their submission and acceptance of his decision because his knowledge encompasses what no scholar can encompass.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p234/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | prefers | He says the best explanation of the unspecified knowledge is God’s statement that he knows the unseen of the heavens and earth. | mentions 2:33

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p240/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | In Arabic, successive quoted statements normally need no conjunction marking sequence because their semantic order is clear; he cites the dialogue about the angels and Adam and many Quranic examples. | mentions 2:30, 2:32, 5:27, 2:259, 2:260, 26:10
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#2/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | للملائكة attaches to قال, and ل is the particle of communication.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#2/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · بعضهم | reports | One etymology makes ملك a form فعَل from الملك with original mīm; on this account only its plural فعائلة is irregular.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#2/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · بعضهم | reports | Another original-mīm derivation starts from ملأك with an extra hamza like شمأل; its vowel shifts to the lām and the hamza drops, while the plural preserves the original addition.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#2/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · بعضهم | reports | A third derivation makes mīm extra and derives the word from ألك, to send. Poems with مألكة, بألوك and مألك attest the message sense; the derivation involves metathesis and hamza deletion, with the plural restoring hamza.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#2/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · بعضهم | reports | A fourth analysis derives it from لأك, also meaning to send; the poem فلست لإنسي ولكن لملأك witnesses the form, and the plural restores hamza.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#2/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · بعضهم | reports | A fifth derivation connects ملك to لاكه يلوكه, to turn something over, since an angel turns a message in the mouth; it derives singular ملوك and plural ملاوكة with vowel change, deletion and hamza formation.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#2/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · النضر بن شميل | reports | Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl says ملك has no derivation in Arab usage.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#3/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | The ة in ملائكة marks a feminine plural as in صلادمة, or could be an intensifier as in علامة and نسابة; the author rejects that latter view. Poetry attests rare deletion of the suffix in الملائك.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#3/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | إني جاعل في الأرض خليفة is the quoted content and direct object of قال; إن is closed because it follows قال without a meaning of supposition.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#3/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | When قول means supposition, إن may be opened or closed; a poem closes it despite its sense, apparently following the surface form of قول.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#3/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | General rule: open إن when its clause can replace a verbal noun; close it when it cannot, such as after قول, initially, in a relative clause or circumstantial clause. Both are possible when substitution is ambiguous, such as after فاء الجزاء or إذا الفجائية.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#3/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | If جاعل means خالق, خليفة is its object and في الأرض either attaches to جاعل or is an omitted phrase circumstantially modifying the following indefinite noun.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#3/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari takes جاعل to mean صير, making خليفة the first object and في الأرض the fronted second object.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#3/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | prefers | خليفة can mean an active successor, succeeding the people addressed or the jinn who preceded them; this is stronger because its feminine suffix is regular for the active sense.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#3/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Alternatively, خليفة means one succeeded by each later generation; the feminine suffix is not regular for this passive sense unless the word has become noun-like, as in النطيحة and الذبيحة.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#3/r9] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | The singular خليفة can intend Adam and his descendants collectively, using the ancestor as with tribal names Mudar and Rabi'a; another view understands خليفة as a generic.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#4/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | A reading substitutes خليقة with qāf for the verse’s خليفة.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#4/r10] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The second فيها is governed by يفسد, and يسفك coordinates with يفسد under either parsing.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#4/r11] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الجمهور | reports | The majority read يسفك in the indicative; another reading makes it subjunctive as an answer to the question with أن understood after wāw.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#4/r12] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | An anonymous poem beginning أتبيت ريان illustrates the subjunctive after an understood أن.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#4/r13] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · ابن عطية | reports | Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls the subjunctive governed by واو الصرف, a Kufan term for wāw redirecting inflection to the subjunctive.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#4/r14] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Readings vary between kasra and ḍamma on fāʾ, a ḍamma on the imperfect prefix from أسفك, and a doubled form for intensity.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#4/r15] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | سفك means pouring and is normally used only of blood; Ibn Fāris and al-Jawharī also allow tears, while al-Mahdawī adds scattered speech.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#4/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | خليفة is accusative as the object of جاعل; active participles govern like their verbs and may be annexed to their object for lightness if nothing intervenes.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#4/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | prefers | قالوا governs إذ قال ربك, which al-Samīn identifies as the preferred parsing.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#4/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī takes the hamza in أتجعل as astonishment.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#4/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · unspecified | reports | Another view treats the hamza as confirmation, supported by the poetic question ألستم خير من ركب المطايا.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#4/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو البقاء | reports | Abū al-Baqāʾ calls the question استشهاد: would God place one who corrupts there like those before? Al-Samīn calls this phrasing unusual.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#4/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | If تجعل means create, the first فيها is attached to it and من يفسد is its object.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#4/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | If تجعل means make into, the first فيها is its second object, advanced before من يفسد.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#4/r9] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | من may be a relative pronoun, leaving the following clause without an independent syntactic position; as an indefinite it makes the clause accusative.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#5/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | دماء is the plural of دم; a declinable noun cannot consist of two letters, so the third radical, its final letter, is omitted.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#5/r10] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Al-Samīn takes Ibn ʿAṭiyya to aim at a causal bāʾ with an omitted verb: praise of God occasioned their glorification and sanctification.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#5/r11] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | الحمد is a verbal noun annexed to its object, with subject omitted as بحمدنا إياك; the claim that the noun itself contains a subject is mistaken.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#5/r12] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Grammarians disagree whether a verbal noun used in place of a verb can contain an implicit pronoun.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#5/r13] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | نقدس coordinates with نسبح and is a predicate of نحن; its omitted object is ourselves and our actions.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#5/r14] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | لك may attach to نقدس or نسبح with a causal sense; it may also be redundant (a weak view), transitive, or explanatory as in سقيا لك.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#5/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | The omitted radical may be wāw or yāʾ as in the duals دموان and دميان; the poem uses الدميان.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#5/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Grammarians disagree whether دم follows فَعْل with a quiescent middle radical or فَعَل with it open.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#5/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The deleted radical may disappear and دم be used as shortened دما, as in the cited poem.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#5/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | The mīm of دم may also be geminated; an anonymous poem uses دمك in that form.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#5/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The underlying plural is الدماو or الدماي; its final weak letter becomes hamza after an extra final alif, as in كساء and رداء.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#5/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The wāw is circumstantial; ونحن نسبح is a nominal clause in the accusative as a circumstantial clause.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#5/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | prefers | بحمدك attaches to an omitted circumstantial phrase: they glorify accompanied by praise, two nested circumstantial states.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#5/r9] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | An alternative makes the bāʾ causal and attaches it to تسبيح; Ibn ʿAṭiyya treats the phrase as an interpolated acknowledgment of God's guidance.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#6/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | prefers | The estimate تقديسنا لك suits the context better than estimating أعني.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#6/r10] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | تقديس means purification, as in الأرض المقدسة, بيت المقدس, and روح القدس.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#6/r11] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | An anonymous poem uses ثوب المقدس for a garment purified for its wearers.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#6/r12] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī derives تقديس from traveling far in the land, making its sense close to تسبيح.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#6/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · ابن عطية | reports | Ibn ʿAṭiyya accepts placing ونحن نسبح inside an implied question: وأنحن نسبح أم نتغير.

[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#6/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الأخفش | reports | A poem’s طربت وما شوقا إلى البيض أطرب is also analyzed with an omitted hamza.

[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#7/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The clause إني أعلم ما لا تعلمون occupies the accusative position as content of قال.

[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#7/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | Al-Samīn rejects the noun analysis as resting on weak premises: أفعل meaning فاعل without comparison and governing like an active participle.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#7/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Another analysis takes أعلم as comparative with منكم omitted and ما as object of implied علمت, since the comparative does not govern it.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#7/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | An anonymous poem is analyzed with القوانس governed by an implied ضرب, not by أضرب.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#7/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | Applying that analysis here requires deleting both the comparison phrase and the verb governing ما, making the ellipsis remote.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30#7/r9] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The contraction is compared with إنا معكم earlier in the sūra. | mentions 2:14
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | إذ is a past-time adverb that shifts a present verb into the past, is indeclinable because it resembles a particle in form and dependence, and may be followed by clauses; fronting a noun before the verb in a verbal clause is awkward.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30/r10] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو عبيد | reports | A fifth analysis treats إذ as redundant, attributed to Abu Ubayd.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30/r11] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | A sixth analysis gives إذ the meaning قد.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30/r12] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | A seventh makes إذ predicate to an omitted subject; an eighth governs it by an implied ابتدأ خلقكم. The author rejects both since creation's beginning was not the time of the statement, and إذ is indeclinable.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30/r13] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | A ninth proposal governs إذ with an implied أحياكم; it is rejected because the two events occurred at different times.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | إذ is not declinable except when attached to a time noun, is not a direct object despite many grammarians' analysis, and is not a place adverb, redundant, causal particle or suddenness particle.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | When the clause governed by إذ is omitted and understood, tanwin compensates for it and kasra avoids two sukuns rather than marking inflection; the author rejects al-Akhfash's alternative. | mentions 56:84
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الأخفش | rejects | Al-Akhfash says the original was وأنت حينئذ, with حين omitted while its genitive remains; the author calls this weak. | mentions 8:67
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | قال ربك is a verbal clause in the genitive because it is annexed to the temporal adverb.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | prefers | Of nine analyses of إذ, the best and simplest makes it governed by قالوا أتجعل فيها: the angels said this at the time God said إني جاعل في الأرض خليفة.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | One proposal governs إذ by an implied اذكر; the author has already rejected making إذ itself a direct object.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | A proposal links إذ to خلقكم in 4:1 and calls the wāw redundant, but the author dismisses it because of the long distance. | mentions 4:1
[SAMIN-DURR:2:30/r9] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | A proposal makes the later قال govern إذ, but this fails because a mudaf ilayh cannot govern its mudaf.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p216/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | God honors Adam's descendants by mentioning them to the highest assembly before creating them; the verse tells Muhammad to recall this and recount it to his people.
